concepts.label: Braking the shot after acceleration
concepts.short_definition: As you accelerate, make the braking at the end of the shot more pronounced. The harder you hit, the more your shoulder, elbow, wrist, and hand work together to stop the motion.
concepts.evidence_summary: As acceleration and hitting force increase, make the braking at the end of the shot more pronounced and coordinate the shoulder, elbow, wrist, and hand to stop the motion.

evidence.excerpt: When you want to accelerate, the feeling of "braking" the shot at the end must be more pronounced. It means the harder I hit, the more my shoulder, elbow, wrist, and hand must work together to abruptly stop the motion after acceleration, like a crisp salute.
evidence.reason: As you accelerate, make the braking at the end of the shot more pronounced. With a harder hit, coordinate your shoulder, elbow, wrist, and hand to stop the motion abruptly.

concepts.label: Compact motion for heavy spin
concepts.short_definition: Starting around the waist and accelerating toward the table shortens the motion and helps produce the explosive snap needed for heavy spin.
concepts.evidence_summary: A high backswing lengthens the downward path and makes acceleration smooth and unconcentrated. Starting around the waist and accelerating toward the table shortens the motion; explosive snap is needed for heavy spin.

evidence.excerpt: A high backswing makes the downward path too long. This large motion makes acceleration smooth and unconcentrated, eliminating the explosive snap needed for heavy spin. Start around the waist and accelerate toward the table to shorten the motion.
evidence.reason: The captions explain that a high backswing lengthens the downward path and smooths out acceleration, then recommend starting around the waist and accelerating toward the table to shorten the motion.

concepts.label: Compact response to a fast ball
concepts.short_definition: Reduce backward pull as the ball gets faster; receiving lessons also call for no backswing and a small swing amplitude.
concepts.evidence_summary: One lesson says faster balls need less backswing and permits lowering the hand without pulling backward. Another warns that pulling the arm back can mistime serve contact, send a strongly spinning short serve long or into the net, and jam the player on a long serve; its first receive principle is no backswing. With imperfect timing, staying close to the ball is said to improve the landing rate. A fast-or-jamming-ball passage warns against instinctively backing away and links being slow with failing to complete the stroke. Another lesson prohibits a large backswing on a fast ball or while moving, with a separate middle-ball contact-point example. A loop-after-serve and receive-loop passage calls for smaller swing amplitude and says these points matter when receiving fast sidespin–backspin.

evidence.excerpt: The faster the ball, the less backswing the speaker recommends. Avoid pulling the arm backward to connect with the ball. Lowering the hand is still permitted, provided it is not pulled backward.
evidence.reason: Reduce backward pull for faster balls; lowering the hand does not itself count as a backswing.

evidence.excerpt: The speaker says timing is often imperfect and that staying close to the ball in those moments gives a much higher chance of landing the shot.
evidence.reason: Stay close to the ball when timing is imperfect.

evidence.excerpt: For receiving serves, the speaker says no technique needs a backswing. Pulling the arm back can mistime contact: on a strongly spinning short serve, the push may go long or into the net; on a long serve, the player can get jammed. For sidespin–topspin, a backswing fights the combined spin. The stated first receive principle is no backswing.
evidence.reason: Avoid a receive pullback that can mistime contact or jam the player on a long serve.

evidence.excerpt: The speaker calls no backswing the first principle of receive and repeats the instruction: no backswing motion.
evidence.reason: Use no backswing motion when receiving.

evidence.excerpt: In discussing receiving a serve when the ball is fast or popping up, the speaker warns that the ball can go long and returns to the first key point: do not take a backswing.
evidence.reason: Avoid a backswing for the stated fast-or-popping-up receive.

evidence.excerpt: For a deceptive no-spin or float ball that looks like backspin but has little spin, the speaker calls for some brushing with a more compact motion, a closed racket angle and force from back to front.
evidence.reason: For the stated deceptive no-spin ball, brush with compact motion, a closed angle and forward force.

evidence.excerpt: For fast or jamming balls, do not instinctively back away. Match the frequency and speed up the motion; the speaker says a slow response leaves the player jammed and unable to finish the stroke.
evidence.reason: Match the pace rather than backing away from fast or jamming balls.

evidence.excerpt: The speaker says smaller movements increase speed and warns that pulling back turns the action into a jump. In discussing increased speed at the table, the speaker calls for small adjustments and warns that adding a pull makes mistakes too easy.
evidence.reason: Use small adjustments for speed at the table and avoid the extra pullback warned about in the lesson.

evidence.excerpt: Do not take a large backswing when the ball is fast or while moving. For amateurs, the speaker prioritizes sound, efficient technique and gives a separate middle-ball example: a huge backswing prevents finding the right contact point.
evidence.reason: Avoid a large backswing for fast balls or while moving; the middle-ball example warns about missing the contact point.

evidence.excerpt: The speaker says both the loop after serve and the receive loop need a smaller swing with very small amplitude, and calls these points crucial for receiving fast sidespin–backspin.
evidence.reason: Keep swing amplitude small for the stated fast sidespin–backspin receive.

concepts.label: Finger-led small-arc shot
concepts.short_definition: A shot in which the fingers lead the wrist and arm through a small arc.
concepts.evidence_summary: The fingers lead the wrist and arm through a small arc; the leading finger differs between shakehand and penhold grips.

evidence.excerpt: For shakehand, the index finger leads; for penhold, the middle finger leads. The fingers should lead the wrist and arm to create a small arc.
evidence.reason: For shakehand, lead with the index finger; for penhold, lead with the middle finger. Let the fingers lead the wrist and arm through a small arc.

concepts.label: Compact stroke under fast rallies
concepts.short_definition: Keeping body or racket movement small in fast exchanges, with separate cues for shorter distances, controlled power and a fast-serve long-ball example.
concepts.evidence_summary: Fast-exchange lessons emphasize compact body or racket movement and avoiding a pulled-back hand. A further looping cue warns against excessive reach. Another lesson calls for an even smaller action for sidespin, and separately calls for a smaller stroke when the distance shortens. Power control is tied to recovery; compact motion after a powerful loop is tied to connecting shots. In a fast-serve long-ball example, the speaker limits upper-arm movement and relies on the forearm and wrist, but uses both “fixed” and “rotate” for the wrist without clarifying their relationship.

evidence.excerpt: In the blocking and counterattacking exchange, the speaker tells the learner to match a faster player’s speed and observe that player’s compact body movement, then emphasizes movement precision.
evidence.reason: Observe the faster player’s compact body movement while matching the exchange speed, and attend to precision.

evidence.excerpt: When the opponent is quick with their forehand and backhand, we shouldn't pull our hand back or make large movements.
evidence.reason: When the opponent is quick with forehand and backhand, avoid pulling the hand back or making large movements.

evidence.excerpt: While discussing increasing speed, the speaker instructs the player to avoid reaching too far while looping and keep the racket compact.
evidence.reason: Avoid reaching too far when looping, and keep the racket compact.

evidence.excerpt: Make your action smaller. Because it's a sidespin, keep it even smaller. You're still using a long stroke; when you hit here, it goes out. The distance has shortened, so you need a smaller stroke as well.
evidence.reason: At the shorter distance, use a smaller stroke.

evidence.excerpt: Table tennis is a back-and-forth game. Control your power to recover properly, and maintain compact form. After a powerful loop, keep the motion compact; otherwise you will not be able to connect shots.
evidence.reason: Control power to recover properly. Maintain compact form; after a powerful loop, compact motion is needed to connect shots.

evidence.excerpt: For the opponent’s fast serve, described as this type of long ball, use less upper arm and rely on forearm and wrist strength without swinging wildly. The passage says the wrist should be “fixed,” then says it “must rotate”; the intended relationship between those two cues is unclear.
evidence.reason: This fast-serve long-ball example limits upper-arm movement and wild swinging; its wrist wording includes both “fixed” and “rotate” without resolving how the two relate.

evidence.excerpt: The speaker says the more power you use, the smaller the motion should be. Do not enlarge the action to hit hard; too much motion and force cause errors. Control the swing size.
evidence.reason: Keep the motion small when applying power instead of enlarging the swing.

evidence.excerpt: The speaker says smaller movements increase speed and warns that pulling back turns the action into a jump. In discussing increased speed at the table, the speaker calls for small adjustments and warns that adding a pull makes mistakes too easy.
evidence.reason: Use small adjustments for speed at the table and avoid the extra pullback warned about in the lesson.

concepts.label: Compact swing with late acceleration
concepts.short_definition: A compact swing with a short backswing can still produce good speed through late, mainly arm-driven acceleration, with little body rotation or movement.
concepts.evidence_summary: A short backswing and late acceleration can produce good speed with little body rotation. Modern forehand guidance also favors a compact position and backswing; when moving, a compact loop helps with footwork, contact-point adjustment, and consistency.

evidence.excerpt: A compact swing with a short backswing and late acceleration can still produce good speed without much body movement.
evidence.reason: Use a compact swing and short backswing, then accelerate late to send the ball with good speed and little body movement.

evidence.excerpt: Modern pros use compact forehand strokes close behind the hip, with no large backswing, and drive their body forward through the ball.
evidence.reason: Keep the forehand position compact near the hip, avoid a large backswing, and drive forward through the ball.

evidence.excerpt: Modern looping technique requires a more compact swing because you need to move your feet and find the right contact point; keep the backswing from getting too large so you can maintain consistency while moving.
evidence.reason: When looping against backspin, keep the backswing compact so you can move your feet, adjust the contact point, and maintain consistency while moving.

concepts.label: Complete motion
concepts.short_definition: Finish the stroke from start to end; stay calm and don't rush.
concepts.evidence_summary: Finish the stroke from start to end; stay calm and don't rush. Complete the friction, hip drive, arm wrap, and forward motion.

evidence.excerpt: The stroke should keep its form by finishing from start to end properly; stay calm and do not rush.
evidence.reason: Finish the stroke from start to end, stay calm, and do not rush.

evidence.excerpt: I am executing a complete, full motion. Complete the friction, the hip drive, the arm wrap, and the forward motion.
evidence.reason: Complete the friction, the hip drive, the arm wrap, and the forward motion.

concepts.label: Consistency
concepts.short_definition: A table-tennis principle of maintaining rally continuity through compact, balanced play rather than brute force.
concepts.evidence_summary: Continue the rally with compact, balanced play, valuing consistency over brute force.

evidence.excerpt: Table tennis is about continuity: continue the rally, keep your body compact, stay balanced, and prioritize consistency over brute force.
evidence.reason: Consistency means continuing the rally with compact, balanced play instead of relying on brute force.

concepts.label: Contact point height for power loop
concepts.short_definition: For a power loop, keep the contact point at table height or slightly above; do not let it drop below the table.
concepts.evidence_summary: At contact, be at table height or slightly above; for a power loop, do not let the contact point drop below the table.

evidence.excerpt: At contact, stay at table height or slightly above; to make a power loop, do not let the contact point drop below the table.
evidence.reason: A backswing may be below the table, but contact should be at table height or slightly above. Contact below the table makes a high, spinny loop; for a power loop, keep the contact point from dropping below the table.

concepts.label: Contact point
concepts.short_definition: The position and timing at which the racket meets the ball.
concepts.detailed_definition: Contact-point examples cover both bounce-phase timing and spacing. Robot practice varies contact on the rise, at the peak and on the fall. A backhand lesson keeps contact in front without becoming jammed or reaching too far, while a fast-serve example places contact close to the body and table.
concepts.evidence_summary: Contact timing depends on the incoming ball. In the soft-ball example, slow down with the ball and allow it to come closer before pressing forward. Timing, balance, and positioning can cause mistakes that appear to be stroke-technique problems.

evidence.excerpt: With only a robot, deliberately practice different contact points: on the rise, at the peak and on the fall.
evidence.reason: Vary bounce-phase contact timing in the stated robot practice.

evidence.excerpt: The speaker identifies the very beginning of descent as the optimal contact point for a heavy-backspin ball.
evidence.reason: Use the early-descent timing cue in this heavy-backspin lesson.

evidence.excerpt: The summary pairs an outward looping arc with contact in the early descending phase.
evidence.reason: Keep the early-descending contact cue in this summary.

evidence.excerpt: With every step, strive to find the optimal contact point because a proper stroke requires a stable body.
evidence.reason: Find a contact point that permits a stable body through the stroke.

evidence.excerpt: Brush the falling ball to synchronize forces. The speaker warns that hitting or brushing backspin at the peak goes into the net, and recommends amateurs let it start dropping after the peak.
evidence.reason: Use the descending-ball contact cue in this backspin example.

evidence.excerpt: Keep backhand contact in front of the body and do not let it drift too far from your center.
evidence.reason: Adds side-specific spacing limits: too close jams the stroke, while too far removes power.

evidence.excerpt: Close to the table, the speaker gives two choices: take the ball on the rise or at the peak.
evidence.reason: Use the two bounce-phase choices stated for close-table play.

evidence.excerpt: When close to the table, the speaker calls flicking on the rise the only real choice.
evidence.reason: Use the close-table, on-the-rise flick cue in this example.

evidence.excerpt: Let the ball come close to the front of the leg before striking. The speaker identifies that area as the contact point for transferring power.
evidence.reason: Use the front-of-leg contact reference described here.

evidence.excerpt: Adjust racket height to the ball, keeping the racket higher than the ball and contacting with the bottom half.
evidence.reason: Use the stated racket-height and bottom-half contact cues in this example.

evidence.excerpt: The speaker says bottom-half contact keeps the ball low. Adjust racket position to each ball height, with the hand slightly higher than the ball rather than the racket lower.
evidence.reason: Adjust racket height to preserve the contact arrangement described in this lesson.

evidence.excerpt: Lower the brushing contact point. The speaker applies this to the forehand side, describing a smoother loop from the lower point and easy net errors when brushing higher.
evidence.reason: Use the lower brushing-contact cue without assigning an unseen exact height.

evidence.excerpt: The speaker introduces why players cannot find their precise hitting position when moving their feet, especially during matches.
evidence.reason: The lesson identifies finding the hitting position while moving as its topic.

evidence.excerpt: The speaker says players cannot lock onto the hitting point because they commit before judging what the opponent gives them.
evidence.reason: Judge the incoming ball before committing in this diagnosis.

evidence.excerpt: The speaker identifies poor sensitivity to spatial adjustments and difficulty locking onto the point, even after finding the position.
evidence.reason: Recognize the spatial-adjustment problem described here.

evidence.excerpt: The speaker says match ability will not improve without locking in timing and point.
evidence.reason: Lock in timing and point as required in this match-ability diagnosis.

evidence.excerpt: In the described progression, once pushes are error-free and the contact point is solid, the coach permits explosive loops with power.
evidence.reason: Keep both push-consistency and solid-contact-point conditions for this progression.

evidence.excerpt: The speaker calls this an anticipation problem: the player has not adjusted to the ball trajectory and found the correct contact point, ending up too high or too low.
evidence.reason: Adjust to the trajectory and locate the return contact point in this diagnosis.

evidence.excerpt: After serving, the speaker starts lightly and first finds the contact point instead of forcing power from a bad position.
evidence.reason: Find the contact point before forcing power in this after-serve example.

evidence.excerpt: Find the contact point first. As the level improves, mix loops and pushes; the forehand-loop example stays at no more than 50% power to avoid renewed tension and keeps focus on the contact point.
evidence.reason: Keep the contact-point focus and stated power limit when adding the forehand loop in this progression.

evidence.excerpt: The progression is push, attack from one wing, lightly loop from both wings, then focus on finding the contact point and adding quality step by step.
evidence.reason: Add contact-point focus and quality within the stated training progression.

evidence.excerpt: Stay calm against a soft ball and slow the action when the ball slows, instead of rushing to take it too early; the same timing principle is applied to topspin looping.
evidence.reason: Stay calm against a soft ball and slow the action when the ball slows, instead of rushing to take it too early; the same timing principle is applied to topspin looping.

evidence.excerpt: Wait an extra moment for the ball to come closer to the body before pressing forward. Timing, balance, and positioning can cause mistakes that look like technique problems.
evidence.reason: Wait an extra moment for the ball to come closer to the body before pressing forward. Timing, balance, and positioning can cause mistakes that look like technique problems.

evidence.excerpt: The practice example changes rhythm from fast to slow.
evidence.reason: The practice example changes rhythm from fast to slow.

evidence.excerpt: After the backswing, the motion and combined force go forward. The speaker locates backswing and contact, then diagnoses deliberately lifting the arm too much after contact.
evidence.reason: Distinguish the contact location from the diagnosed excessive upward motion after it.

evidence.excerpt: An overly fast backswing puts the contact point too far in front, making continuous shots difficult.
evidence.reason: Avoid the too-fast backswing and far-forward contact combination described here.

evidence.excerpt: The spinnier the ball, the lower the speaker lets it drop. The lesson contrasts knee-height control with waist-height power looping and recommends knee-height contact rather than waist height.
evidence.reason: Keep the lesson-specific contrast between lower contact for control and waist-height power looping.

evidence.excerpt: Wait for the ball to drop to the indicated area before swinging, with a natural, calm and controlled rhythm.
evidence.reason: Wait for the ball to drop before swinging, with a calm and controlled rhythm.

evidence.excerpt: A shorter space between backswing and contact makes the contact point easier to find.
evidence.reason: Keep the backswing-to-contact space short in this example.

evidence.excerpt: The forehand-drive space from takeback to contact stays compact regardless of standing position, and the speaker says to use the peak of the bounce.
evidence.reason: Use the compact takeback-to-contact space and peak timing stated for the forehand drive.

evidence.excerpt: The speaker says the rhythm for chopping, flicking or slicing in this example is at the peak of the bounce.
evidence.reason: Keep the peak timing attached to the actions named in this example.

evidence.excerpt: After a very spinny serve brings back a low soft push, the speaker gives two options: step in and loop at the peak, or wait for descent and loop with heavy spin. The lesson warns against power looping at descent.
evidence.reason: Keep the low soft-push condition and distinguish peak contact from descending heavy-spin contact.

evidence.excerpt: For a half-long ball coming past the table, the speaker offers stepping in to loop at the peak or waiting for the drop and looping with spin at a lower point.
evidence.reason: Choose between the two stated half-long-ball timing options.

evidence.excerpt: Complete the stroke, then move the feet to the forehand position for the next shot. The speaker says the body should be still at contact for every stroke.
evidence.reason: Separate completing the stroke from the next foot movement in the stated drill.

evidence.excerpt: Contacting the ball too early causes the racket to meet it with the bottom part, leading to missed or powerless contact and ineffective friction.
evidence.reason: Wait for the drop rather than contacting too early with the bottom of the racket and losing effective friction.

evidence.excerpt: The coach explains that standing too close restricts the stroke and recommends moving the point of contact slightly farther from the body horizontally.
evidence.reason: Move the contact point slightly farther from the body horizontally to avoid a restricted stroke.

evidence.excerpt: The speaker calls the peak the optimal topspin contact point, then clarifies that peak refers to starting the forward swing, rather than actual ball contact.
evidence.reason: Start the forward swing at the peak; the speaker distinguishes that from actual ball contact.

evidence.excerpt: If you feel you're pushing forward, your contact point is too early; pushing sideways indicates a broken wrist, while needing to lift the ball suggests you're being jammed.
evidence.reason: Pushing forward indicates early contact, sideways pushing indicates a broken wrist, and needing to lift indicates being jammed.

evidence.excerpt: The lesson asks why loops against backspin hit the net, then compares upper-half racket contact in a forehand drive, with a normal trajectory, against lower-half contact that dives down. The speaker says lower contact can send the loop into the net.
evidence.reason: In this comparison, upper-half contact gives the drive a normal trajectory, while lower-half contact sends the ball down and can put the loop into the net.

evidence.excerpt: Bring the ball to the front-right, at most chest height, and stop there to leave room for the arm to accelerate afterward.
evidence.reason: Stop at the front-right point, no higher than the chest, leaving room for the arm to accelerate afterward.

evidence.excerpt: The speaker compares a rising contact that feels urgent and poorly coordinated with a peak contact described as more coordinated.
evidence.reason: The peak-contact example feels more coordinated than the urgent rising-contact example.

evidence.excerpt: For a high topspin shot, the speaker places contact more upward. When the center of gravity is lower, brush at that point; after lifting it, the spin is stronger.
evidence.reason: When the center of gravity is lower, brush at the more upward point and lift for stronger spin in this high-topspin example.

evidence.excerpt: In serving, accurately locating the contact point on the ball improves the outcome; positioning the ball too far from the body makes it difficult to find the correct side contact point.
evidence.reason: Position the serve ball close enough to find its side contact point accurately.

evidence.excerpt: When receiving the curving serve, find the ball contact point quickly and stay focused. The speaker locates the points on the left side and refers to the indicated point.
evidence.reason: Track the curving serve and locate its contact point in this receive example.

evidence.excerpt: For a fast serve, the contact point should be close to the body and near the table, with a low center of gravity, to produce a high-quality long ball.
evidence.reason: For the fast serve, use contact close to the body and table with a low center of gravity.

evidence.excerpt: The speaker distinguishes the ready position from the point where racket and ball meet.
evidence.reason: Distinguish ready position from racket-ball contact.

evidence.excerpt: Forehand and backhand loops against backspin are more difficult because the distance between the ball and the racket has to be extremely precise.
evidence.reason: Loops against backspin require extremely precise distance between the ball and racket.

evidence.excerpt: The primary key point for beginner forehand stances is achieving a contact point toward the front.
evidence.reason: Choose a beginner forehand stance that permits contact toward the front.

evidence.excerpt: For hitting, contact around 2:00; contacting at 1:00 sends the ball into the net and requires a more open racket.
evidence.reason: For hitting, contact around 2:00; open the racket more if 1:00 contact sends the ball into the net.

evidence.excerpt: Focus on the contact point.
evidence.reason: The speaker explicitly instructs the player to focus on the contact point.

evidence.excerpt: The speaker says a defensive block is performed on the rise and places block contact in front. Against sidespin-topspin, the lesson says to hit at the highest point with an upright elbow and vertical racket.
evidence.reason: Preserve the separately stated defensive-block and sidespin-topspin timing cues.

evidence.excerpt: Keeping the loop tight to the body helps find the contact point when moving.
evidence.reason: Keep the loop tight to the body to find the contact point when moving.

evidence.excerpt: The contact point for a forehand topspin loop and a drive are different.
evidence.reason: The forehand topspin loop and drive use different contact points.

evidence.excerpt: For serving, the speaker refers to the demonstrated contact point and says not to “open up the friction.”
evidence.reason: The captions name contact and an instruction about friction but do not specify an exact contact location or racket angle.

evidence.excerpt: The speaker contrasts lower-half racket contact, likely to hit the net, with center contact using power to overcome spin and upper-half contact for brushing.
evidence.reason: Keep these racket-face contact outcomes as the lesson’s stated contrast.

evidence.excerpt: For these short half-high balls, you have to hit them at the peak of the bounce.
evidence.reason: Hit these short half-high balls at the peak of the bounce.

evidence.excerpt: The speaker diagnoses poor spin from an incorrect contact position: brushing on the upper portion of the racket, combined with poor brushing technique, makes the ball bounce off the blade.
evidence.reason: The speaker diagnoses upper-racket contact and poor brushing technique together as making the ball bounce off the blade.

evidence.excerpt: The speaker says contact is too high and the ball rises further when hit from top to bottom. After serving, use a held racket as a height reference and do not exceed it.
evidence.reason: Use the height of the held racket as a reference after serving so the contact point stays low enough.

evidence.excerpt: The speaker explains that contacting below the ball while moving upward produces topspin, while contacting during a downward racket motion produces mostly backspin.
evidence.reason: Upward racket travel from below the ball produces topspin; downward travel at contact produces mostly backspin.

evidence.excerpt: For a high topspin shot, the speaker places contact more upward. When the center of gravity is lower, brush at that point; after lifting it, the spin is stronger.
evidence.reason: With a lower center of gravity, brush at the more upward point and lift the ball for stronger spin in this example.

evidence.excerpt: The racket is relaxed before striking, and the point of contact is where the ball and racket meet.
evidence.reason: Keep the racket relaxed before striking and meet the ball at the racket-ball contact point.

evidence.excerpt: Meet the ball in front for backspin, topspin, pushes, flicks and defense. In the backhand-backspin explanation, lifting alone can net the ball and the speaker calls for forward force.
evidence.reason: Meet the ball in front across the named strokes; the backspin explanation also calls for forward force.

evidence.excerpt: The speaker diagnoses force applied from the second half of the swing, contact too far back and insufficient forward force, then calls for being close to the ball and applying friction when striking.
evidence.reason: Avoid contact too far back with insufficient forward force; stay close to the ball and apply friction when striking.

evidence.excerpt: Contact is just the beginning of the stroke; the speaker treats contact as the real start rather than the endpoint.
evidence.reason: Treat contact as the start of the stroke rather than hesitating there after forcing the early motion.

evidence.excerpt: The lesson names contact as its topic, refers to the demonstrated hand shape, and says the contact point is on the lower part of the racket.
evidence.reason: Use the lower part of the racket as the contact point in this lesson.

evidence.excerpt: In a sidespin example, the speaker draws attention to the visible contact point, refers to contact “here,” and then calls for a brushing motion.
evidence.reason: Attend to the contact point and then apply brushing in this sidespin example.

evidence.excerpt: In this stable rally, both players synchronize timing and hit at the peak. The speaker explicitly says it is not an attack-versus-defense drill.
evidence.reason: Synchronize both players at peak contact in this stable rally, which is not an attack-versus-defense drill.

evidence.excerpt: For looping on the falling point, start the racket hand below table level and make contact to the side of the body, never behind it.
evidence.reason: For falling-point looping, start the hand below table level and contact beside the body rather than behind it.

concepts.label: Contact zone on the ball
concepts.short_definition: Choosing where on the ball’s surface to contact, with source-specific spin, serve and brushing cues.
concepts.detailed_definition: Contact examples distinguish bottom or lower-middle contact for backspin, back contact for a flat fast serve, and middle-back contact for left sidespin without added backspin. The lesson’s vertical scale calls bottom contact maximum spin, lower-middle strong spin, and middle or upper-middle minimum spin. A driven-serve example uses a point halfway between back and side, followed by deception, while distinguishing brushed short serves from driven long serves. Another lesson describes finger-driven brushing across multiple points using “1D to 3D” contact language.
concepts.evidence_summary: The contact examples map specific ball regions to backspin or sidespin cues and include a back-then-side contact sequence that avoids the bottom. A driven example contacts halfway between back and side and adds the fake follow-through afterward. Separate finger-action passages contrast one-point contact with brushing across multiple points. An upper-middle brushing cue appears with a forward lunge into a loop.

evidence.excerpt: Contact the bottom or lower-middle of the ball to produce backspin.
evidence.reason: In this contact cue, the lesson assigns backspin to bottom and lower-middle contact on the ball.

evidence.excerpt: For a flat fast serve, contact the back of the ball. For left sidespin, use the middle-back and avoid the bottom half to produce clear sidespin without backspin.
evidence.reason: The lesson distinguishes back contact for the flat fast serve from middle-back contact for left sidespin without backspin.

evidence.excerpt: For sidespin without backspin, hit the back first and then the side rather than the bottom. The speaker warns that continuing to hit the bottom will not produce topspin, regardless of practice.
evidence.reason: The contact sequence is back first, then side; the passage contrasts this with continued bottom contact and its failure to produce topspin.

evidence.excerpt: The lesson’s contact-zone map describes bottom contact as maximum spin, lower-middle contact as strong spin, and middle or upper-middle contact as minimum spin.
evidence.reason: This vertical contact-zone scale is the lesson’s comparison of maximum, strong and minimum spin.

evidence.excerpt: In the driven-serve example, contact halfway between back and side of the ball and drive through that spot with the racket angle, for either penhold or shakehand. Add the deceptive follow-through after driving. The speaker separately contrasts brushed short serves with driven long serves and allows different fakes after the drive.
evidence.reason: The example puts contact halfway between back and side for both grips, then adds deception after the drive; its short/long serve distinction is stated separately.

evidence.excerpt: The speaker says that without finger movement, contact hits one point and the ball leaves too fast. With finger movement, the speaker describes contacting a third to a half of the ball’s surface and calls this “1D to 3D contact.”
evidence.reason: The speaker contrasts one-point contact without finger movement with the broader contact described when the fingers move.

evidence.excerpt: At contact, the fingers drive the racket face to brush across multiple points. The lesson contrasts hitting one point throughout the stroke with finger-driven faster grazing across one, two and three points.
evidence.reason: Use the fingers to drive the racket face into the multiple-point grazing action described here, rather than one-point contact throughout the stroke.

evidence.excerpt: While addressing the inability to reach even a short ball, the lesson calls for lunging forward to loop and brushing the ball’s upper-middle region.
evidence.reason: The reach-correction cue combines a forward lunge into a loop with upper-middle brushing.

concepts.label: Control before power
concepts.short_definition: Control the power level and match the incoming rhythm before trying to finish the point with force.
concepts.evidence_summary: One lesson matches the opponent’s push rhythm using 50% power; another says to synchronize first and then explode. A backhand-practice lesson uses about 50% strength while focusing on control and touch. Other examples prioritize putting the receive on the table and building consistency before developing a finishing power loop.

evidence.excerpt: A fast push can be matched, while responding too fast to a slow push fails. The speaker attributes many misses to timing and rhythm rather than heavy spin, and warns against using one motion and speed regardless of the opponent’s rhythm.
evidence.reason: Match the incoming push rhythm rather than imposing one speed; the speaker distinguishes timing errors from heavy-spin errors.

evidence.excerpt: Mismatched tempo can leave a player reaching or jammed. The speaker then says to control the power level first and use 50% power.
evidence.reason: Control power at the stated 50% level in this tempo-matching lesson.

evidence.excerpt: Match the rhythm of the opponent’s push. For a slow push, push slowly and then loop with 50% power, staying with the opponent’s rhythm.
evidence.reason: Use the stated push-rhythm and 50%-power loop cue rather than going fast against a slow push.

evidence.excerpt: If the opponent pushes fast, follow that speed. Focus on the opponent’s rhythm rather than your own form, using the stated 50–60 power level.
evidence.reason: Follow the fast-push rhythm using the speaker’s stated 50–60 power cue.

evidence.excerpt: Put sensitivity on the opponent rather than your own swing: match a fast serve fast and slow play slowly.
evidence.reason: Attend to the opponent’s tempo instead of concentrating only on your own swing.

evidence.excerpt: Follow the opponent’s fast-push speed and rhythm using the stated 50–60 power level. The passage also includes the speaker’s prediction of improvement and a clearer grasp of rhythm.
evidence.reason: The passage gives the 50–60 power rhythm cue and separately includes the speaker’s prediction of improvement.

evidence.excerpt: The speaker calls it ball-control ability: using balance, body weight and footwork to find the correct position for every ball.
evidence.reason: Use balance, weight and footwork to find the correct position for each ball, as described in the lesson.

evidence.excerpt: Reducing power a little is described as raising consistency; slowing things down is linked to gaining real attacking ability.
evidence.reason: The speaker links reduced power and a calmer pace to consistency and attacking ability.

evidence.excerpt: Control power and focus on putting the ball on the table. After serving, do not focus on generating power immediately; the speaker directs this advice to beginners with one to three years’ experience.
evidence.reason: Keep the stated beginner and post-serve condition when prioritizing table contact over immediate power.

evidence.excerpt: For the speaker’s forehand heavy-spin loop, use no more than 50% power; going beyond that is said to bring tension back. Focus on finding the contact point. The backhand choice in this example is a push.
evidence.reason: Preserve the forehand heavy-spin-loop example and its no-more-than-50% power limit.

evidence.excerpt: Slow down and match rhythm and spacing first rather than trying to smash every slightly high ball. Reducing power is described as improving consistency, with a calmer pace leading toward attacking ability.
evidence.reason: Establish rhythm and spacing before forcing power in the stated example.

evidence.excerpt: Change playing rhythm for different balls and find a suitable receiving position. Against an opponent who pushes aggressively, use a compact stroke to keep up with the pace.
evidence.reason: Match the stated aggressive-push pace with a compact stroke and suitable receiving position.

evidence.excerpt: If the opponent pushes slowly, loop slowly too; the speaker calls this matching the backswing to the ball. Being fast against a slow opponent causes mistakes, while fast play calls for a fast response.
evidence.reason: Match the backswing and stroke rhythm to the opponent’s slow or fast play.

evidence.excerpt: For beginners with one to three years’ experience who cannot attack well after serving, push first, slow the pace and stay calm. Find the contact point first, then mix loops and pushes as the level improves.
evidence.reason: Retain the beginner, post-serve and unreliable-attack conditions for pushing first and progressing later.

evidence.excerpt: If the opponent’s return is not very strong, find the contact point and defend first to settle into rhythm. Begin making a full stroke as the level improves.
evidence.reason: For the stated weaker return, defend and settle into rhythm before progressing to a full stroke.

evidence.excerpt: First push, then attack from one wing, then lightly loop from both wings. Find the contact point and add quality step by step.
evidence.reason: Use the stated staged training sequence rather than forcing quality immediately.

evidence.excerpt: The speaker says slowing down can leave the opponent as the one rushing and making errors.
evidence.reason: The lesson describes a consequence of slowing down; it does not promise a winning shot.

evidence.excerpt: The speaker attributes almost all misses in this explanation to rushed rhythm rather than excessive spin.
evidence.reason: The speaker’s stated diagnosis is rushing the rhythm, not heavy spin.

evidence.excerpt: Matching rhythm does not prevent power: synchronize first, then explode.
evidence.reason: The speaker explicitly puts rhythm synchronization before the powerful release.

evidence.excerpt: Do not try to win with one loop; land it, then play the point.
evidence.reason: Prioritize landing the loop and continuing the point rather than forcing an immediate winner.

evidence.excerpt: Against a heavy, fast serve, adjust the strategy from trying to crush the push to simply getting it back. The opponent may push again rather than punish it.
evidence.reason: For the stated heavy-fast serve, choose the described return-first strategy rather than trying to finish with one push.

evidence.excerpt: Serve receive is not meant for maximum quality; the first priority is getting the ball on the table.
evidence.reason: Put table contact first in the speaker’s serve-receive priority.

evidence.excerpt: For slow, soft, floating balls, stay alert, compact and ready. Wait until settled into position before hitting rather than swinging while still moving.
evidence.reason: Keep the slow-soft-floating-ball condition for alert readiness and settling before the swing.

evidence.excerpt: Stop moving before striking. Treat tricky soft balls as difficult rather than easy; if spinny, push back. Stay mentally alert, track the ball and stay close.
evidence.reason: Preserve the spinny-ball push alternative and close tracking in this soft-ball lesson.

evidence.excerpt: Use the speaker’s out-of-ten principle: if the opponent gives eight, give two; five, give five; two, give eight.
evidence.reason: The speaker presents these complementary contributions as the out-of-ten principle.

evidence.excerpt: After serving, leave a forearm’s distance. If the opponent blasts the ball, borrow the speed and redirect; if the ball is soft, generate your own power. Do not retreat first.
evidence.reason: Preserve the fast-versus-soft distinction and the speaker’s stated post-serve spacing and no-retreat-first cues.

evidence.excerpt: Backhand strokes need a clear breaking direction and ending position. The speaker contrasts an opponent’s 70% with a 30% response against both players using 70%, which is called uncontrollable, and says to adjust to incoming ball speed rather than mirror power.
evidence.reason: For this backhand example, adjust the contribution to incoming speed instead of matching force one-for-one.

evidence.excerpt: The speaker applies pressure only when very confident. In a backhand example, the speaker says, “If he is just a bit faster,” they would not choose to apply force, emphasizing stability and finding the right moment.
evidence.reason: In this backhand example, added force is conditional on confidence; the speaker declines it in the stated faster case and emphasizes stability and the right moment.

evidence.excerpt: In backhand practice, use about 50% strength, avoid brute force and focus on ball control and touch. Avoid inconsistent strength.
evidence.reason: Keep the backhand-training condition for the stated 50% strength and control-and-touch emphasis.

evidence.excerpt: Do not rush. Open the racket angle slightly and wait for an opportunity before applying power; the speaker defines the opportunity here as a half-high return from long pips.
evidence.reason: Keep the long-pips half-high-return condition for the stated power opportunity.

evidence.excerpt: Leave margin for error and first get the ball over the net and onto the table; then consider adding quality and spin.
evidence.reason: The speaker prioritizes margin and table contact before additional quality or spin.

evidence.excerpt: Focus on consistency now; address quality later.
evidence.reason: The speaker separates the present consistency focus from later quality work.

evidence.excerpt: For this loop example, the speaker barely opens the forearm, stays close and contacts at the peak to land the ball. Find the technique that gives you consistency, then develop a finishing power loop.
evidence.reason: Build consistency first, preserving the speaker’s specific forearm, spacing and peak-contact example rather than a universal loop prescription.

concepts.label: Control power rather than maxing out
concepts.short_definition: Generate power with control while keeping the ball on the table.
concepts.evidence_summary: Generate power with control instead of blindly hitting, and keep the ball on the table. Practice power control at 30%, 50%, and 80% of maximum power.

evidence.excerpt: Generate power with control instead of blindly hitting, while keeping the ball on the table.
evidence.reason: Use controlled power rather than blindly hitting, and keep the ball on the table.

evidence.excerpt: The second fundamental skill is power control: practice hitting at 30%, 50%, and 80% of your maximum power.
evidence.reason: Practice power control at 30%, 50%, and 80% of your maximum power.

concepts.label: Control rhythm through spacing and recovery
concepts.short_definition: Coordinating spacing and stroke timing to maintain rally rhythm, including room for the backswing and avoiding recovery before the stroke is finished.
concepts.evidence_summary: Leave backswing room and avoid rushing underspin balls. One lesson links rushed timing to starting recovery before finishing the stroke; another describes mismatched rhythms and progressively faster hitting ending rallies. A pushing-and-looping practice passage links rhythm and stability with footwork transitions, space control and stroke form.

evidence.excerpt: Create space after each shot and leave room for the backswing. Time forehand and backhand backswings using the body’s movement time; rushing underspin balls will not give good results.
evidence.reason: Create space after each shot for the backswing, use the body’s movement time, and avoid rushing underspin balls.

evidence.excerpt: Understanding spacing improves rhythm; the lesson explains rushed timing as starting recovery before finishing the stroke.
evidence.reason: Avoid starting recovery before the stroke is finished; the lesson links this premature recovery to rushed timing.

evidence.excerpt: First ensure stroke-framework stability, rhythm and a sense of space. The lesson recommends pushing mixed with looping to train push rhythm, stability, footwork transitions, space control and stroke form.
evidence.reason: Pushing mixed with looping is described as harder than serve-and-attack practice and useful for training rhythm, stability, transitions, space control and stroke form.

evidence.excerpt: The lesson explains that mismatched rhythms can make two players uncomfortable: when one is fast and the other a beat slow, timing suffers. Rushing faster and faster destroys the rhythm and ends the rally after a few shots.
evidence.reason: The lesson describes mismatched player rhythms causing timing problems, and progressively faster hitting disrupting rhythm and ending the rally after a few shots.

concepts.label: Counter-loop
concepts.short_definition: A stroke called a “forward spin shot” in one lesson, with separate source-specific examples of incoming-ball selection, loop rhythm and extended-rally strategy.
concepts.evidence_summary: One lesson describes counter-loop force from back to front and contrasts it with lower-right-to-upper-left force for what it calls a topspin loop. Another chooses counter-loop for a high, slow, low-quality incoming ball and topspin for a low, fast ball. Related loop-rhythm cues compare the rhythm with backspin, suggest room about a meter from the table and a clear pause, and say to slow down against topspin to avoid rushing. A forehand timing example waits for rhythm to allow waist, hips and arm to combine. A strategy example recommends extended counter-looping rallies for a physically strong, solid player.

evidence.excerpt: For a physically strong, solid player, the speaker recommends extending rallies and entering counter-looping exchanges.
evidence.reason: The extended-rally counter-looping strategy is recommended here for a physically strong, solid player.

evidence.excerpt: The speaker compares the rhythm with that used against backspin and calls for slowing down. For looping, the lesson says standing about one meter from the table gives time to make the stroke.
evidence.reason: In this loop-rhythm cue, slow down and leave the approximately one-meter distance described as giving time for the stroke.

evidence.excerpt: If you do not want to rush the timing on your loop, first slow yourself down against topspin.
evidence.reason: The cue for avoiding rushed loop timing against topspin is to slow down first.

evidence.excerpt: Try standing a little farther back so the rhythm has a clear pause. The speaker says to look at the rhythm and feel the timing.
evidence.reason: Stand a little farther back for the clear pause described in this rhythm cue.

evidence.excerpt: Even while accelerating, taking the ball slightly early on the forehand side is described as preventing the waist and hips from generating power properly. Wait for the rhythm to have time to rotate the waist, drive the hips and finish the arm to combine forces.
evidence.reason: For this early forehand-contact problem, the lesson recommends waiting for rhythm so waist, hips and arm have time to combine.

evidence.excerpt: The lesson calls the counter-loop a forward spin shot with force from back to front. It contrasts this with lower-right-to-upper-left force for what it calls the topspin loop, identifying force direction as the main difference.
evidence.reason: In this lesson’s terminology, the counter-loop’s back-to-front force is contrasted with a lower-right-to-upper-left topspin-loop force.

evidence.excerpt: After considering the opponent’s incoming-ball quality, the lesson chooses a counter-loop for a high, slow, low-quality ball and calls topspin more reasonable for a low, fast ball.
evidence.reason: This selection cue distinguishes high, slow, low-quality incoming balls from low, fast ones, using the lesson’s counter-loop and topspin labels.

evidence.excerpt: In this lesson, a high, slow, low-quality incoming ball is selected for a counter-loop, while a low, fast ball is selected for topspin.
evidence.reason: This lesson’s selection cue contrasts high, slow, low-quality balls with low, fast ones.

concepts.label: Create space and avoid jamming
concepts.short_definition: When the ball jams you and makes you feel you must lift, move farther from the table—about an arm’s length away—and keep the compact backhand in front of your body.
concepts.evidence_summary: Feeling compelled to lift can indicate that the ball is jamming you. Move farther from the table, about an arm’s length away, and keep the compact backhand in front of your body.

evidence.excerpt: If you feel you must always lift up, you're getting jammed by the ball. To fix this, position yourself further from the table, about an arm's length away, and understand the backhand is a compact stroke executed in front of your body.
evidence.reason: If you feel you must lift the ball, move about an arm’s length from the table and keep the compact backhand in front of your body.

concepts.label: Create space for the stroke
concepts.short_definition: For power, keep your hand from getting too close to the ball; for a loop, rotate your torso during preparation to avoid getting jammed.
concepts.evidence_summary: Keeping the hand too close to the ball limits power. For a loop, rotating the torso during preparation helps avoid getting jammed and brings the contact point in front and to the right of the body. From their experience, one speaker maintains about one forearm of distance from their body when hitting a backhand drive and says that distance is suitable.

evidence.excerpt: If your hand is too close to the ball, you won't be able to generate power effectively.
evidence.reason: Keep your hand from getting too close to the ball to generate power effectively.

evidence.excerpt: To avoid getting jammed on a loop, rotate your torso as you prepare; this brings the contact point in front and to the right of your body.
evidence.reason: Rotate your torso as you prepare for the loop to avoid getting jammed and bring the contact point in front of your body.

evidence.excerpt: When I hit a backhand drive, I maintain about one forearm of distance from my body through the backswing, hit, and recovery. That distance is very suitable.
evidence.reason: On a backhand drive, the speaker maintains about one forearm of distance from their body through the backswing, hit, and recovery, and calls that distance suitable.

concepts.label: Cross-court loop to forehand from middle
concepts.short_definition: On a middle ball, loop cross-court to the opponent's forehand for a longer trajectory and more margin, while extending the stroke and pulling the opponent out of position.
concepts.evidence_summary: Looping cross-court to the opponent's forehand gives a longer trajectory and more margin for error. On a middle ball, it allows a full stroke and can pull the opponent out of position.

evidence.excerpt: Looping cross-court gives a longer trajectory and more margin for error. On a middle ball, I loop to the opponent's forehand, fully extend my stroke, and pull them out of position.
evidence.reason: The cross-court loop offers added trajectory and margin while letting the player extend the stroke and pull the opponent out of position.

concepts.label: Curved serving motion and ball path
concepts.short_definition: The serve explanations address both movement and ball flight: a forward-pivot cue, a curved flick with a light tap, and a sideways-curving ball that makes the receiver adjust.
concepts.evidence_summary: One explanation says 'The movement follows this arc' and calls for a forward pivot corresponding to the serve trajectory, rather than a straight forward or downward hit. Another calls for a curved flick, subtle force, and a light tap. A third explains that a sideways-curving serve makes the opponent adjust and is harder to return than a straight ball.

evidence.excerpt: The instruction is 'The movement follows this arc', contrasted with stepping forward or hitting forward or downward. A forward pivot is needed; the speaker says this pivot corresponds to the serve trajectory, which is neither straightforward nor linear.
evidence.reason: The instruction 'The movement follows this arc' is followed by a required forward pivot, which the speaker connects to a serve trajectory described as neither straightforward nor linear.

evidence.excerpt: The serving explanation calls for a curved flick, then subtle force and a light tap, with the cue to 'keep it in front of you'.
evidence.reason: Use a curved flick followed by subtle force and a light tap; the accompanying position cue is to 'keep it in front of you'.

evidence.excerpt: A straight serve is easy for the opponent to aim at, but a serve that curves to the side is less straightforward to hit and becomes difficult to return.
evidence.reason: A straight serve is easy to aim at. If the ball deviates or curves sideways, the opponent needs to adjust, making it harder to return.

concepts.label: Deceptive flick
concepts.short_definition: A flick for balls with more spin that starts with a push; push forward before flipping the racket to press down. It can also be used on a falling ball.
concepts.evidence_summary: The shot starts with a push. Push forward before flipping the racket to press down, since flipping too early leaves the shot affected by backspin. The flick can also be used on a falling ball.

evidence.excerpt: Start with a push, push forward through contact, then flip the racket to press down. This flick can also be used on a falling ball.
evidence.reason: Push forward first, then press down; flipping too early leaves the shot affected by backspin. The flick can also be used on a falling ball.

concepts.label: Deceptive follow-through
aliases: follow-through that makes the racket face appear to open
concepts.short_definition: The speaker describes adding a deceptive follow-through that makes the racket face appear to open.
concepts.evidence_summary: An added deceptive follow-through makes it look as though the racket face is opening.

evidence.excerpt: They add a deceptive follow-through that makes it look like the racket face is opening.
evidence.reason: The speaker describes the apparent racket-face opening produced by an added deceptive follow-through.

concepts.label: Deep push against heavy backspin
concepts.short_definition: In this passage, the speaker recommends a deep push against heavy backspin and describes the flick under discussion as suited to half-spin and topspin.
concepts.evidence_summary: In this passage, the speaker recommends a deep push against heavy backspin and describes the flick under discussion as suited to half-spin and topspin.

evidence.excerpt: In this passage, the speaker says flicking heavy backspin gives the opponent a lob, then recommends a deep push. The speaker describes the flick under discussion as suited to half-spin and topspin.
evidence.reason: The speaker recommends a deep push against heavy backspin and describes the flick under discussion as handling half-spin and topspin.

concepts.label: Defense as interception and redirection
concepts.short_definition: Defense centers on interception and redirection rather than counter-hitting.
concepts.evidence_summary: Defense centers on interception and redirection rather than counter-hitting.

evidence.excerpt: At its core, defense is about interception and redirection, not counter-hitting.
evidence.reason: Defense centers on intercepting and redirecting the ball rather than counter-hitting.

concepts.label: Defensive block against long fast serves
concepts.short_definition: Against a long fast serve, use a defensive block to absorb its incoming power instead of adding your own force.
concepts.evidence_summary: For a long fast serve, use a defensive block to absorb its power. Adding your own power when receiving a fast serve can send the ball off the table. For many sidespin-topspin serves, start with a controlled block instead of a big swing.

evidence.excerpt: To return a long fast serve, block it like a defensive shot and absorb its power.
evidence.reason: When receiving a fast serve, adding your own power can send the ball off the table. For many sidespin-topspin serves, start with a controlled block instead of a big swing.

concepts.label: Defensive positioning after pushing
concepts.short_definition: After pushing, recover to cover the opponent’s likely cross-court first attack: cover your own backhand corner after pushing to their backhand, or cover the cross-court angle after pushing to their forehand.
concepts.evidence_summary: After pushing, recover to cover the opponent’s likely cross-court first attack: cover your own backhand corner after pushing to their backhand, or cover the cross-court angle after pushing to their forehand.

evidence.excerpt: The opponent’s first attack will generally be cross-court. After pushing to their backhand, quickly cover your own backhand corner; after pushing to their forehand, quickly cover the cross-court angle.
evidence.reason: After pushing to the opponent’s backhand, quickly cover your own backhand corner; after pushing to their forehand, move to cover the cross-court angle.

concepts.label: Defensive positioning to cover the cross-court
concepts.short_definition: After serving, prepare to cover the opponent’s cross-court return.
concepts.evidence_summary: Lock down the cross-court angle: after serving to the opponent’s backhand, immediately prepare to cover the cross-court return to your backhand; after serving to the forehand, cover the cross-court forehand.

evidence.excerpt: After serving, immediately prepare your position to cover the cross-court return.
evidence.reason: After serving, prepare to cover the cross-court return.

evidence.excerpt: If you serve to their backhand, prepare to cover the cross-court return to your backhand. If you serve to the forehand, cover the cross-court forehand.
evidence.reason: After serving to the opponent’s backhand, immediately prepare to cover the cross-court return to your backhand; after serving to the forehand, cover the cross-court forehand.

concepts.label: Changing rhythm against blocking and stepped-back defense
concepts.short_definition: After a short loop, use a direct hit on the next ball rather than looping repeatedly. A separate example says that if the opponent steps back to defend, a soft ball with spin can hinder the counterloop; close-table blocking is a different case.
concepts.evidence_summary: One cue says to pause then loop; another follows a short first loop with a direct hit rather than another loop, warning that repeated looping can become passive. After a heavy-spin loop is blocked, the next hit makes the rhythm hard to follow. Against an opponent who steps back to defend, soft balls are troublesome if they carry spin; the passage distinguishes this from close-table blocking.

evidence.excerpt: The cues are to pause then loop, and after a short first loop to make the second ball a direct hit. Do not loop again after the first loop, or it is easy to become passive.
evidence.reason: After a short first loop, make the second ball a direct hit rather than another loop. The passage also gives a pause-then-loop cue.

evidence.excerpt: After a heavy-spin loop is blocked, hit the next ball so the rhythm becomes hard to follow.
evidence.reason: Follow the blocked heavy-spin loop with a hit to make the rhythm hard to follow.

evidence.excerpt: Close-table blocking is a different case. If the opponent steps back to defend, soft balls are troublesome; as long as the ball has spin, the opponent will not easily counterloop.
evidence.reason: Against stepped-back defense, use the source's soft-ball condition with spin; close-table blocking is explicitly a different case.

concepts.label: Grip firmly at contact on the flick
aliases: grip firmly when brushing the ball
concepts.short_definition: For the flick, grip the racket firmly the instant you brush the ball; squeezing only at the very end is too late.
concepts.evidence_summary: For a flick, grip the racket firmly as you brush the ball. Squeezing only at the very end is too late and will send the ball into the net.

evidence.excerpt: For a flick, grip firmly as you brush the ball; squeezing only at the end of the swing is too late.
evidence.reason: For a flick, grip firmly as you brush the ball. If you wait until the end of the swing to squeeze, the ball will hit the net.

concepts.label: Diagonal step-in for forehand
concepts.short_definition: For forehand balls, step in diagonally. Stepping in straight can leave you jammed by a slightly deeper ball.
concepts.evidence_summary: For the forehand, step in diagonally. Stepping in straight can let a slightly deeper ball jam you.

evidence.excerpt: For the forehand, step in diagonally. If you step in straight, a slightly deeper ball will jam you.
evidence.reason: Step in diagonally for the forehand; stepping in straight can let a slightly deeper ball jam you.

concepts.label: Reading the opponent and ball
concepts.short_definition: Reading the opponent’s action and the incoming ball before committing to a response.
concepts.evidence_summary: The lessons connect observation with stroke choice and preparation. One warns against drawing back before reading the opponent’s action. Another starts movement when the opponent commits to a stroke direction, with adjustments for wide and narrow angles. Ball-tracking instruction follows the trajectory from racket to racket. Serve-return examples compare the spin expected after spin and no-spin serves and call for a corresponding looping method. A separate cue reads the landing point and trajectory before the body rises.

evidence.excerpt: Committing before judging the incoming ball can leave the player between a push and a loop when a half-long ball proves longer than expected.
evidence.reason: The lesson describes drawing the hand back before judging the ball, then changing between two decisions.

evidence.excerpt: After serving, recover quickly with the hands in front of the chest, then read the opponent’s action before committing. Even for a forehand ball, avoid drawing back immediately.
evidence.reason: The speaker says drawing back early loses the force connection.

evidence.excerpt: Start moving when the opponent commits to a stroke direction. Extend for a wide angle and adjust by yielding for a narrower angle toward the middle.
evidence.reason: The speaker contrasts this with waiting until the ball is already on the player’s side.

evidence.excerpt: Observe the opponent’s take-back to distinguish winding up for power from preparing to bump the ball. Earlier reading gives more time to prepare the player’s own shot.
evidence.reason: The speaker contrasts a rushed loop after slow observation with time to prepare a power loop after quick observation.

evidence.excerpt: Track the ball with the eyes and get into position with the body turned sideways to create the proper angle.
evidence.reason: The lesson also distinguishes contacting a power loop out in front from letting a high, spinny loop drop closer to the body.

evidence.excerpt: The speaker describes turning sideways, tracking the ball into the hitting zone and following it back out through the stroke, from the opponent’s racket to the player’s and back.
evidence.reason: The narration connects eye tracking with accurate contact and encourages following the entire trajectory.

evidence.excerpt: The lesson says a push returned after a spin serve has relatively strong spin, while the return after a no-spin serve has relatively weak spin; sidespin is described as following the same principle.
evidence.reason: The speaker uses the server’s spin choice to explain the spin expected on a push return.

evidence.excerpt: After a half-spin or no-spin serve, the lesson says little spin remains after the bounce and the pushing opponent mostly borrows the server’s spin rather than adding it actively. Use a corresponding method to loop the returned spin.
evidence.reason: The speaker asks the player to understand how the serve affects the return before choosing the looping method.

evidence.excerpt: After a heavy-underspin serve, the opponent’s push borrows that spin; the speaker warns that the server’s own spin can cause mistakes.
evidence.reason: This example attributes the spin on the pushed return to the heavy-underspin serve.

evidence.excerpt: See the ball clearly before moving, set the feet before the hand acts, and be stable before striking.
evidence.reason: The instruction asks the player to control the impulse to rush and move only after reading the ball.

evidence.excerpt: When receiving, focus on the ball’s position, keep the body stable, and shift after spotting the position.
evidence.reason: The speaker asks the receiver to identify the position before shifting.

evidence.excerpt: In this receiving exercise, the speaker directs the red side forward and to the right for right spin, then asks for a slight adjustment to the left against left spin.
evidence.reason: The leftward adjustment is explicitly kept small rather than exaggerated.

evidence.excerpt: In rallies, read the opponent’s intention. The speaker asks whether the player can spot an impending direction change as the opponent releases the shot.
evidence.reason: The question focuses attention on the opponent’s action at shot release.

evidence.excerpt: The speaker asks whether the player can judge when the speaker makes a move and whether the ball is far away or close.
evidence.reason: The speaker asks the player to judge movement and the ball’s distance.

evidence.excerpt: Read the landing point, trajectory and motion before the body rises.
evidence.reason: The speaker says movement is ineffective while crouched and places the rise after reading the ball.

concepts.label: Stroke size for ball speed, distance and footwork
concepts.short_definition: Use a compact backswing for a fast ball and for a slow ball close to the table. With a slow ball, use a slightly larger backswing at mid-distance and increase it proportionally farther back, without making it too large. More foot movement calls for a smaller backswing.
concepts.evidence_summary: Use a compact backswing for a fast ball and for a slow ball close to the table. With a slow ball, use a slightly larger backswing at mid-distance and increase it proportionally farther back without making it too large. Use a smaller backswing when moving your feet more.

evidence.excerpt: For a fast ball, use a compact backswing. For a slow ball, stay compact close to the table, use a slightly larger backswing at mid-distance, and increase it proportionally farther back without making it too large. More foot movement calls for a smaller backswing.
evidence.reason: Match backswing size to the ball and your position: keep it compact for a fast ball or a slow ball close to the table; for a slow ball, enlarge it gradually as you move farther back, while keeping it controlled. Reduce it when moving your feet more.

evidence.excerpt: When moving the feet and transitioning from backhand to forehand, the body is already generating force; adding a large backswing causes errors. More foot movement calls for less backswing. Keep the motion compact without pulling the hand too far back.
evidence.reason: Use less backswing as foot movement increases; avoid adding a large pullback during the transition.

concepts.label: Distance management for hitting range
concepts.short_definition: One arm’s distance is the proper hitting range; near the baseline, the stroke gets jammed.
concepts.evidence_summary: One arm’s distance is the proper hitting range; near the baseline, the stroke gets jammed.

evidence.excerpt: One arm’s distance is basically the proper hitting range. Near the baseline, your stroke gets jammed.
evidence.reason: Use one arm’s distance as the proper hitting range; near the baseline, your stroke gets jammed.

concepts.label: Downward pressure and friction on serve
concepts.short_definition: On a serve, apply downward pressure at ball contact to increase friction; without this pressure, the contact produces more impact and less friction.
concepts.evidence_summary: Apply downward pressure on the ball to increase friction; without pressing down, contact produces more impact and less friction. Against a blocker, it changes placement before spin and speed, then power. Another cue waits after the opponent’s push and strikes suddenly. A training example gives the intended action a command when intent disrupts the stroke. A separate placement rule goes crosscourt if the opponent stays still after pushing and down the line if they anticipate crosscourt.

concepts.label: Forehand loop power generation
concepts.short_definition: Generate forehand-loop power through racket-head motion, with loop lessons also describing body-led preparation and acceleration.
concepts.detailed_definition: One lesson explicitly calls the body-led action a loop: open the arm, let body rotation lead the backswing while the hand stays in front, then accelerate. Another lesson drops down, drives forward and brakes the arm, calling forward drive essential when looping. A separate loop-power example uses friction followed by forward force while standing still without using the body.
concepts.evidence_summary: Examples include body-led preparation, a drop-drive-brake sequence, acceleration paired with braking, and forehand-loop racket-head motion. After a no-spin serve returns half-long and slightly high, one lesson permits a power loop; its high-ball example uses mainly impact with brushing as a supplement. Another loop-power example uses friction followed by forward force while standing still without body power.

concepts.label: Practice intensity, timing and coordination
concepts.short_definition: Exercises for reduced-power practice, arm-and-body coordination, contact timing and variable feeds. Some examples specifically concern loops; others use shadow practice or varied topspin-rally feeds.
concepts.detailed_definition: In one fixed-point drill, a partner blocks with either forehand or backhand and the learner uses about 40–50% strength without standing too close. Another lesson recommends 30–40% power for amateurs before technique and structure are stable. A shadow-practice cue first coordinates arm and body, then uses racket swings without hitting before ball training. Separate drills alternate rising and early-descending contact or vary feed speed, height, pace and placement.

concepts.label: Forehand loop spacing and contact zone
concepts.short_definition: Preserve enough room from the table and body for the ball to enter a repeatable contact zone without reaching or getting jammed.
concepts.detailed_definition: Good spacing is dynamic rather than a single fixed distance. Start far enough from the table to complete the stroke, adjust with the feet to the ball's depth, and let the ball approach the lead-leg area so body rotation can transfer power without overreaching.
concepts.evidence_summary: Good forehand loop spacing starts from a practical base distance and a compact preparation that can be adjusted with left-right weight shifts. The contact point should stay in front of the body, with enough space to avoid being jammed, and the player should maintain roughly arm's length from the table when needed to execute the stroke cleanly.

concepts.label: Forehand loop swing path and racket angle
concepts.short_definition: The racket travels on an outer arc while a suitably closed face brushes and drives through the ball.
concepts.detailed_definition: A loop is not merely a larger drive. The racket head follows an outer arc, covers the ball with a closed face, and moves forward through contact. The precise balance of impact and brush changes with incoming spin, height, and the desired arc.
concepts.evidence_summary: The forehand loop swing path should cover the ball with a stable diagonal racket face rather than a purely vertical brushing motion. The forearm drives forward and up through contact, the racket head starts the acceleration, and the motion stays compact and controlled so the ball is lifted with forward drive instead of being sent long or into the net.

concepts.label: Forehand loop timing and rhythm
concepts.short_definition: Time the forehand loop with source-specific cues for waiting, incoming pace and bounce phase.
concepts.detailed_definition: Timing cues vary by the ball and practice setting. One continuous forehand topspin lesson uses early descent; another topspin example uses peak or rising contact. One push example allows peak or rising contact only for a slow push when already positioned. A rhythm lesson uses wait, loop for a slow ball and wait, quick for a fast ball.
concepts.evidence_summary: Continuous forehand topspin practice uses early descent, while another topspin example describes contact at the peak or on the rise. A backspin lesson permits peak-or-rise contact only for a slow push when already in position. Other examples adjust backswing speed to incoming pace, delay pulling back until the ball is understood, or use relaxed preparation before late acceleration.

evidence.reason: Stay relaxed while approaching the ball, then apply force just before contact.

concepts.label: Post-shot recovery and spacing
concepts.short_definition: Recovery of the body and hands, compact movement to reduce recovery time, and post-shot spacing. In a fixed-point drill, return in place to the ready position immediately after hitting.
concepts.evidence_summary: One spacing cue says to step back after hitting and leave an arm’s length of space. The examples call for body-and-hand recovery and quick recovery after backhand topspin and forehand play. In a fixed-point drill, return to ready position in place immediately after hitting rather than waiting for the return. A backhand-to-forehand transition cue avoids dropping the arm before resetting. Against slow long-pips returns, recover quickly but do not rush or use inverted-rubber rhythm; stay low and lean forward. A separate video describes the speaker’s straight-back recovery, contrasts circular recovery and gives a personal preference for comfort.

evidence.excerpt: After hitting the ball, take a step back and leave an arm’s length of space.
evidence.reason: This spacing cue is to step back after the shot and leave an arm’s length of room.

evidence.excerpt: After finishing one, the lesson goes through recovery at a stable rhythm. If the rhythm is too fast, movements can be incomplete and the shot has no quality. The lesson calls for body rotation and hand movement in a complete body-and-hand recovery.
evidence.reason: Use the body rotation and hand movements described for complete recovery; the lesson warns that overly fast rhythm can leave movements incomplete and the shot without quality.

evidence.excerpt: For example, after a backhand topspin, don't freeze your hand. Recover. Return quickly. Always recover. Same with the forehand.
evidence.reason: After a backhand topspin, return quickly rather than freezing the hand; the same recovery cue is given for forehand play.

evidence.excerpt: The lesson says a big motion takes longer to recover from, asks for a smaller and more focused movement, and says to remember recovery and let the body follow through.
evidence.reason: Use the smaller, focused movement described here and remember to recover; the lesson says a larger motion takes longer to recover from.

evidence.excerpt: After every shot, you must recover to the ready position. Players who fail to recover lose space to generate power. Every shot must return to your backswing position; only then does your backhand have quality.
evidence.reason: The backhand cue calls for recovery after each shot, warns that missed recovery loses power-generating space, and says returning to the backswing position gives backhand quality.

evidence.excerpt: Recover quickly but do not rush: the ball from long pips comes slowly, so do not use inverted-rubber rhythm. Stay low and lean forward.
evidence.reason: For the slower long-pips ball, recover quickly without rushing, stay low and lean forward rather than using inverted-rubber rhythm.

evidence.excerpt: In a fixed-point drill, recover in place to the ready position immediately after hitting: “hit, then recover.” Do not wait to see the return or for the ball to come back before starting recovery.
evidence.reason: For this fixed-point drill, use immediate in-place recovery after the hit rather than waiting for the returning ball.

evidence.excerpt: To maintain a continuous loop, actively recover as soon as you finish the stroke, resetting immediately and treating the sequence as one complete motion.

concepts.label: Early stroke preparation and timing cues
concepts.short_definition: In a topspin example, the speaker reports feeling rushed and being unable to generate power if the backswing starts only after the bounce, and calls for the body to be prepared before the ball arrives. evidence.excerpt: If I only start my backswing after a topspin ball bounces on my side, I won't be able to generate power and I'll feel rushed. Before the ball reaches you, your body is already prepared. Then power comes easily.
